open-question.question: The build is to accept slot values held in files beside the inline [slots] table of a host's settings.toml. How does a definition bind a file to a slot name, and where do the files live: discovered by a fixed naming convention under a fixed directory of the definition, named explicitly per slot in the TOML, or another binding, and at which path? (The binding form and the location constrain each other, so both are asked together.)

When a host definition supplies the same slot both inline in its [slots] table and as a file-backed value, what does the build do: refuse the definition, or let one of the two forms take precedence, and which?
open-question.alternative: The build refuses a definition that supplies one slot both inline in [slots] and as a file-backed value, whatever the two values hold. The refusal is a BuildError raised while load_definition reads the definition, before anything renders, and it names the slot and both sources. No precedence rule exists. It matches the build's posture today, where every malformed definition (unknown key, non-string value, reserved name, stray placeholder) is refused at load. Every slot then has exactly one place its value comes from, so an editor never changes a value that the build silently ignores. Moving a value from inline to a file has to happen in one edit, deleting the inline entry in the same change, because an intermediate state with both fails the build. It also adds a load-time rule and an error message that the new build test has to cover.

The build accepts a slot supplied in both forms when the two values are identical after the build's normal reading of each, and uses that value. It refuses the definition, at load and naming the slot and both sources, only when the two values differ. A value can be copied into a file and the build checked before the inline entry is deleted, while two forms that disagree still cannot pass silently. The redundant copy is allowed to stay. It turns into a build failure the first time someone edits only one of the two copies, so the second place to edit is never removed, only deferred. Whether "identical" holds also depends on how a file value's trailing newline is read, which the trailing-newline sibling question owns.

The build accepts a slot supplied in both forms and uses the inline [slots] value, ignoring the file-backed one without a failure. The file acts as a default that an inline entry overrides. The definition never fails over this case, and settings.toml stays the one file that shows which value wins. A reader of the TOML sees the value that renders whenever an inline entry is there. A file-backed value can sit in the definition directory and never render. An editor who edits that file sees no change and gets no error, and --check passes because the committed tree was also rendered from the inline value. That is a silent dead copy, in a build that otherwise refuses every malformed definition.

The build accepts a slot supplied in both forms and uses the file-backed value, ignoring the inline [slots] entry without a failure. The inline entry acts as a default that a file overrides. The definition never fails over this case, and a value can be moved into a file and take effect at once, with the leftover inline entry deleted at leisure. The inline value in settings.toml, together with the comment above it explaining that host's value, can be stale and never render. A reader of the TOML is misled about what the tree carries, and the build gives no signal that this is so.

The build adds no duplicate rule of its own. The file-backed form is bound so that one slot can be supplied only once, for example by making the file reference that slot's own [slots] entry, and TOML's own refusal of a repeated key already catches any second entry. There is no new rule, message, or test case. Duplication is ruled out by the definition's structure rather than detected, so neither a refusal path nor a precedence rule has to be written or documented. It is viable only if the binding form chosen by the File-backed slot declaration form sibling gives each slot a single key. Under a binding by naming convention in a directory, or under a separate table, a duplicate can still arise, and with no rule the outcome would come down to an undocumented dictionary-update order.

open-question.question: A text file conventionally ends with a newline while an inline TOML slot value does not. When a file-backed slot value is substituted into a core/ file, are its bytes used verbatim, or is trailing whitespace normalised, and by what rule?
open-question.alternative:
The build reads a file-backed value as UTF-8 text and removes exactly one trailing line ending (a final "
", or "
") if the file ends with one, keeping every other byte as written, earlier trailing newlines and spaces included; a file with no final newline is used as it stands. No check is added for the file's ending. Files can follow the ordinary text-file convention editors and tools enforce, while a value whose meaning needs trailing whitespace (such as the Codex prompt-opener values that today end in "

" inline) can still be held in a file by writing one extra newline, so the file form can carry any value the inline form can and the rule is one sentence long. The file's bytes and the substituted bytes differ by one invisible character, so a reader must know the rule to tell what a file with two final newlines yields, and a value meant to end in exactly one newline needs a file ending in two, which looks like a mistake and invites someone to "fix" it.

The build removes every trailing whitespace character (all final newlines, spaces, and tabs) from a file-backed value before substituting it, keeping leading whitespace and interior bytes verbatim. A value that must end in whitespace cannot be file-backed and stays inline in settings.toml. The most forgiving rule: however an editor or a stray keystroke leaves the end of the file, the rendered tree is the same, so the file ending can never introduce a blank line or a drift diff into a host tree, and the rule matches how the inline multi-line values are written today (closing ''' straight after the last word). A slot whose value legitimately ends in whitespace — today's Codex prompt-opener values end in "\n\n" — can never move to a file, so the two forms are no longer equivalent and the rule constrains which slots may be file-backed, which is the Inline versus file assignment question's to settle; whether this matters depends on that outcome.

The build removes leading and trailing whitespace (blank lines and spaces at both ends) from a file-backed value, keeping interior bytes verbatim, so a file may open or close with blank lines or a comment-free margin. A value that must begin or end in whitespace stays inline. Gives the file author the most freedom in layout — a blank first line, trailing blank lines, any final newline — with one symmetric rule that is easy to state and test. Silently discards leading whitespace too, which no value needs stripped today and which an indented or newline-prefixed value would rely on, so it widens the set of values the file form cannot carry beyond the trailing-whitespace case for no gain the trailing-only rules lack; whether that set matters again depends on the Inline versus file assignment outcome.

The build substitutes a file-backed value's bytes exactly as read, with no normalisation, and the definition loader refuses a value file whose last byte is a newline (failing the build with a message naming the file), so a value file must be saved without a final newline; a value that needs trailing whitespace other than a newline can still be file-backed. What the file holds is exactly what lands in the tree, with no hidden rule for a reader to learn, and a stray final newline is caught at build time rather than surfacing as an unexplained blank line in a rendered host tree. Fights the near-universal convention that text files end in a newline: many editors, formatters, and git's "No newline at end of file" warning push the other way, so value files are awkward to edit and the refusal will fire routinely; and a value that must end in a newline (the Codex prompt openers) cannot be file-backed at all.

The build substitutes a file-backed value's bytes exactly as read, with no normalisation and no check of the file's ending; keeping a value file free of an unwanted final newline is left to whoever edits it. The least build code and the simplest contract: the file is the value, every value the inline form can express (trailing "\n\n" included) can be expressed in a file, and nothing is ever altered behind the author's back. Any editor that appends the conventional final newline silently changes the rendered tree — an extra line break after a paragraph slot, or a broken sentence where a slot sits mid-line — and the drift gate does not catch it, because the rebuilt tree is what gets committed; the error surfaces only in review of the rendered diff, if at all.

open-question.question: Once both forms exist, which slot values are held in files and which stay inline in settings.toml: every value, only the multi-line paragraphs, or whichever each host definition chooses per slot?

The milestone adds a lightweight pytest of the build's rendering. What does that test exercise, and how does it reach the build code: the slot-filling step alone through an import, a full render of a small synthetic core and definition into a temporary directory, or the real build run as a subprocess against the repository's own core/ and hosts/? (What is tested and how the code is reached constrain each other, so both are asked together.)

The Python 3.9 floor run collects the same tests/ directory as the pinned run but has neither PyYAML nor tomllib, both of which the build imports. How is the rendering test kept to the pinned interpreter: a skip inside the test, a collection rule in conftest.py, a location outside the floor run's test paths, or a change to the floor command itself?

Four capability-conditional passages of the alternatives pass are to become slots: the opening paragraph's "where the host allows it", the two repair branches of sub-step e, and the repair-wait sentence. How are they divided into slots (one slot per passage, one slot for the whole repair sub-step, or folded into the existing ALTERNATIVES_CONCURRENCY), and, since a slot value may carry no other placeholder, what becomes of the AGENT_TOOL and ALTERNATIVES_AGENT slots that are used only inside those branches? (The two choices constrain each other, so both are asked together.)
open-question.alternative: Division: one new slot per passage, four in all: the opening paragraph's concurrency phrase, the continue-session branch, the re-dispatch branch, and the repair-wait sentence, with the sub-step e lead-in ("whichever of these two branches the host supports, in this order") reworded in core to name no capability. ALTERNATIVES_CONCURRENCY stays as it is. Agent slots: AGENT_TOOL and ALTERNATIVES_AGENT are removed from all three definitions and their wording is written literally inside each host's branch values, as ALTERNATIVES_DISPATCH already writes the `Agent` tool literally. The build is unchanged apart from the milestone's file-backed values. Each slot replaces exactly the text that varies, so sub-step e keeps its present shape in core and every host value is small and local to the sentence it fills, with no build rule relaxed. Core fixes a two-branch skeleton for every host, so a host whose own mechanism has only one repair path renders an empty or awkward bullet, and the tool name is repeated across two values per host; whether every host has both branches depends on the per-host value-sourcing questions.

Division: the same four per-passage slots as the inline option, with the sub-step e lead-in reworded to name no capability and ALTERNATIVES_CONCURRENCY unchanged. Agent slots: AGENT_TOOL and ALTERNATIVES_AGENT are kept, and the build is changed so a slot value may carry another declared slot placeholder: slot filling runs until no declared placeholder remains (refusing a cycle), and the slot-declaration check counts a slot used only inside another slot's value as used. The tool and agent names stay defined once per host and shared by both branch values, so no wording is duplicated and the existing eight slots survive unchanged. It relaxes a deliberate build rule (a value may carry only `{{PLUGIN_ROOT}}`) and adds a recursive fill, cycle handling, and a changed slot-declaration check for the sake of two short phrases, all of which the new rendering test must then cover.

Division: two new slots. The opening phrase gets its own slot; one repair slot holds the sub-step e lead-in, both branches as the host has them, and the repair-wait sentence, with sub-step e reordered in core so that text is contiguous ahead of the fixed corrective message, its fill rule, and the one-repair cap, which stay in core. ALTERNATIVES_CONCURRENCY stays as it is. Agent slots: AGENT_TOOL and ALTERNATIVES_AGENT are retired and written literally inside each host's repair value. Each host states its whole repair mechanism in one value, with as many branches as it really has, so no host inherits another's two-branch structure, while the host-neutral corrective message and cap stay single-sourced. Sub-step e must be reordered and the repair value grows to a multi-line paragraph per host that repeats shared phrasing (the same-path landing, the last-line verdict) unless that is carefully left in core.

Division: the opening phrase as its own slot and one repair slot holding the lead-in, the branches, and the repair-wait sentence, with sub-step e reordered so the fixed corrective message, fill rule, and cap stay in core. Agent slots: AGENT_TOOL and ALTERNATIVES_AGENT are kept, used inside the repair value, with the build changed to fill slot placeholders inside slot values (repeated until none remain, refusing cycles) and the slot-declaration check counting such use. Gives each host one coherent repair paragraph while keeping the tool and agent names as named, separately commented values per host. Pays the build change for nesting even though both names now occur inside a single value per host, where a literal would cost nothing in duplication.

Division: one new slot for the repair branches (the sub-step e lead-in and both branches as the host has them); the repair-wait sentence is folded into ALTERNATIVES_CONCURRENCY, whose per-host value then says how both first dispatches and repairs are waited on, leaving a host-neutral pointer in sub-step e; the opening phrase is reworded in core to defer to the paragraph opening step 3 rather than slotted. Agent slots: AGENT_TOOL and ALTERNATIVES_AGENT are retired and written literally into each host's repair value. Puts each concern in one place per host, collection and waiting in the concurrency paragraph that already owns them and repair paths in one value, adding only one slot. ALTERNATIVES_CONCURRENCY grows further (already thirteen to twenty lines) and must now describe the repair wait before the reader reaches sub-step e, and the intro no longer says how the dispatches run without a forward reference.

Division: no new slot. ALTERNATIVES_CONCURRENCY absorbs the repair branches and the repair wait, so each host's step-3 opening paragraph states how it dispatches, waits, and repairs; sub-step e in core keeps only the trigger (repair every refused file at once), the fixed corrective message, its fill rule, and the one-repair cap; the opening phrase is reworded in core to defer to step 3. Agent slots: AGENT_TOOL and ALTERNATIVES_AGENT are retired and their wording written literally into each host's concurrency value. Fewest slots: every host-dependent behaviour of the pass lives in one value per host, so a host's whole mechanism can be read and rewritten against a hands-on check in one place. The one paragraph becomes a large multi-topic value that describes repairs before the step that triggers them, splitting the repair procedure between step 3's opening and sub-step e and making the skill harder to follow in order.

Division: only the conditional clauses become slots: the opening phrase, the sub-step e lead-in, each branch's condition clause ("Where the host can continue…", "Where the host cannot…"), and the repair-wait sentence's condition, while the branch bodies stay in core. ALTERNATIVES_CONCURRENCY stays as it is. Agent slots: AGENT_TOOL and ALTERNATIVES_AGENT stay exactly as they are, still used in the core branch bodies, with no build change. The smallest edit to core and to the build: existing slots and the value-may-carry-only-PLUGIN_ROOT rule are untouched, and the shared branch wording stays single-sourced. Slot values become sentence fragments that must read grammatically against core text, and a host cannot drop a branch its mechanism lacks, so every tree still renders both repair branches; it works only if every host's value-sourcing outcome keeps both branches.

open-question.question: The new per-host slots need Claude Code values that describe only that host's own mechanism, yet the goal names a hands-on check for Antigravity alone. Where do the Claude Code values come from: lifted from the arm of today's capability-conditional prose that applies to it, rewritten from a hands-on check of Claude Code as well, or taken from its documentation alone?

The new per-host slots need Codex values for the repair branches and repair wait, which today's Codex definition does not cover. Where do those values come from: derived from Codex's documentation as the existing Codex values were, or rewritten from a hands-on check against the locally installed codex as well?

The Antigravity slot values are to be rewritten from a hands-on check against the installed agy. Where is that check recorded so a later editor can tell what each value was written against: in the comment above each value in the host definition, in the milestone's decisions only, as a repeatable script kept in the repository, or nowhere beyond the values themselves?
open-question.alternative: Recorded in the Antigravity host definition, per value: the comment above each Antigravity slot value in scripts/hosts/antigravity/settings.toml names the agy version the value was checked against and the observed behaviour it rests on (what dispatch, waiting, continuing an agent, or the context file was seen to do). No separate file, script, or CLAUDE.md entry carries the check. The record sits at the exact place an editor changing a value reads, and it extends the existing convention that each slot comment says why this host's value is what it is, so a value written from observation and one written by inference are told apart at a glance. The version is repeated across every Antigravity comment and nothing checks it, so a value edited later without a re-check keeps a stamp that now overclaims, and a newer agy leaves every stamp silently stale; where a value ends up held in a file rather than inline is a condition on whether a comment can sit above it at all (the inline-versus-file assignment and the file-backed binding form are sibling questions).

Recorded in the Antigravity host definition, once: a single block in the header comment of scripts/hosts/antigravity/settings.toml names the agy version and date of the check and lists what was observed; the per-value comments state only what each value describes and why, in mechanism terms, with no version. A later re-check updates one block rather than every comment, and the definition still carries its own evidence where an editor of it looks first. The stamp covers the whole definition, so a single value edited afterwards without a re-check still reads as checked; an editor must connect a value to the header list by hand rather than seeing its basis beside it.

Recorded in this milestone's directory only: the check's agy version and each observation the values rest on are written out deliberately in the milestone's own record (its Decisions and the completing task's Verified entry in TASKS_DONE.md); the host definition's comments keep describing each value in mechanism terms with no version or reference to the check. Adds nothing to maintain: the record is a committed, dated snapshot that never claims to be current, and git blame on a value leads to the milestone commits that wrote it. An editor reading settings.toml sees no sign that a value was observed or against which agy, and must know to dig through history to find it; the milestone files are not where host-definition editors look.

Recorded in CLAUDE.md: the rewritten "Host wording differences are named slots" invariant states that the Antigravity values were written from a hands-on check, names the agy version, and summarises the observed mechanisms they rest on; the host definition's comments carry no version. CLAUDE.md is already the home of rationale and is read at the start of every session, and today's invariant already explains why the Antigravity value is what it is, so the replacement explanation lands where the old one stood. Puts a volatile tool version and behaviour facts into the invariants file, which is meant to hold lasting design decisions, and separates the evidence from the values it covers so the two can drift apart unnoticed.

Recorded as an executable probe kept in the repository (under scripts/): it runs the installed agy's version, help, and agent-listing commands and checks the strings the Antigravity values rely on, and each Antigravity slot comment points at it; the parts of the check it cannot automate are noted in the script beside the commands. A re-check after an agy update is one command rather than a manual investigation, and the evidence can be reproduced rather than taken on trust. Only the static facts (version, flags, help strings, agent listing) are scriptable; dispatch, waiting, and continuing an agent need a live model session that is nondeterministic, billed, and logged in, so the script proves the least important part; it cannot run in CI where agy is absent, adds an untested script to scripts/, and goes stale as silently as a comment.

Not recorded anywhere deliberately: the rewritten values stand on their own, their comments describe each mechanism and why the value is what it is with no version or reference to the check, and the only trace is whatever the routine completion entry and commit history happen to hold. Makes no claim that can go stale, matches how the Codex values are recorded today (their comments cite the mechanism and no version), and adds no artifact to keep in step with agy. A later editor cannot tell what agy the values were written against or whether a value was observed rather than inferred, which is the very uncertainty that left the Antigravity values unchecked until this milestone.

open-question.question: Antigravity's tree today names CLAUDE.md as the context file, while the agy binary names GEMINI.md and AGENTS.md as its rule files and never CLAUDE.md. If the hands-on check confirms that Antigravity reads more than one project instruction file, which one does the Antigravity tree name as its context file?
open-question.alternative: The Antigravity CONTEXT_FILE value stays "CLAUDE.md", as it is today. Only the comment above it is rewritten so that it no longer claims byte-identity with the Claude Code tree. Every one of the roughly thirty CONTEXT_FILE sites, the bootstrap's created file, and the README template's /init sentence keep naming CLAUDE.md. Nothing changes for existing Antigravity projects. A project that runs both Claude Code and Antigravity keeps one shared context file. The skills read the file explicitly by path, so they work whether or not agy loads it on its own. The agy binary names GEMINI.md, AGENTS.md, and .agents/rules/*.md as rule files and never CLAUDE.md. So the workflow section the bootstrap writes would never reach an Antigravity session's context by itself, and agy's /init would document the project somewhere the skills do not read. It also leaves the Antigravity tree naming another host's instruction file, which contradicts the goal that each tree describes only its own mechanism.

The Antigravity CONTEXT_FILE value becomes "AGENTS.md" at the workspace root. The Antigravity and Codex trees then name the same file. The README template's /init sentence is rewritten to name it too. It is one of agy's documented workspace rule paths, and agy's embedded documentation recommends a consolidated AGENTS.md (with GEMINI.md given as the parenthetical alternative, and rules/AGENTS.md recommended inside plugins). As the cross-tool convention, it lets a project used under both Codex and Antigravity keep one environment-context file and one workflow section. The value stays a plain root-level file name, so every "workspace root" sentence and the bootstrap's "# CONTEXT_FILE" heading read correctly without touching core/. If the hands-on check shows that agy's own /init or project setup writes GEMINI.md, a project documented the Antigravity way would hold its context in a file the skills never read. Existing Antigravity projects whose workflow section sits in CLAUDE.md stop being read, which depends on what the context-file transition question decides.

The Antigravity CONTEXT_FILE value becomes "GEMINI.md" at the workspace root. The README template's /init sentence is rewritten to name it too. It is the instruction file agy names first and the one belonging to Antigravity's own model family, so it is the file most specific to this host. It keeps Antigravity's workflow section apart from any AGENTS.md that other tools or Codex maintain in the same project. A project used under both Codex and Antigravity ends up with two environment-context files and two copies of the workflow section, and the two drift apart. agy's embedded documentation recommends AGENTS.md over it. Existing Antigravity projects whose workflow section sits in CLAUDE.md stop being read, which depends on what the context-file transition question decides.

The Antigravity CONTEXT_FILE value becomes a cairn-owned file under agy's workspace rules directory, for example ".agents/rules/cairn.md". It sits beside the .agents/plugins/cairn install path, and the bootstrap creates it there. Because the value is no longer at the workspace root, the core/ sentences that say "at the workspace root" are reworded so they read correctly for a nested path. agy loads every .agents/rules/*.md file, so the workflow section reaches each session. Cairn also never edits a project instruction file shared with other tools or with the project's own /init output, and all of cairn's Antigravity state stays under .agents/. The file is meant to be both the project's environment context, read by derive-tasks, specify-milestone-starting-state, and the completion procedure, and the home of the workflow section. A cairn-owned rules file would hold only the workflow section, so the skills would find no domain context unless the user moves it there. It also needs core/ edits outside the slot, since "workspace root CONTEXT_FILE" and the "# CONTEXT_FILE" heading assume a root-level file name.

No file name is fixed now. The Antigravity CONTEXT_FILE value is whichever root-level file the hands-on check shows agy's own /init (or its project-documenting step) writes, either GEMINI.md or AGENTS.md. The README template names that same file. It keeps the project's own documentation step and the workflow's reads and writes on one file. This is the same reason the Codex value gives for AGENTS.md ("its /init writes that file"), so the slot comment can state a checked fact rather than a preference. The recorded decision is a rule, not a value, so the file name is settled only when the check runs. If agy has no /init or writes neither file, the rule does not resolve and the question reopens. Existing Antigravity projects whose workflow section sits in CLAUDE.md stop being read, which depends on what the context-file transition question decides.

open-question.question: If the Antigravity context file changes away from CLAUDE.md, is any transition provided for existing Antigravity projects whose CLAUDE.md already carries the workflow section, or does the change apply only to projects bootstrapped after it?

If the hands-on check shows that Antigravity loads a plugin's agents only through a manifest or frontmatter fields the agent files do not carry today, does this milestone add what Antigravity needs to its host definition, or do the Antigravity slot values describe a generic-subagent fallback as the Codex ones do?

The new development rule says a rendered tree must never name another host's mechanism. Does it cover only the files rendered from core/, or also the host's own templates (README, CONTRIBUTING pointer, manifest) in the same tree?

Today no slot value names a host, in keeping with the rule that runtime files name no host. Once a slot value describes one host's own mechanism, may it name that host (for example its tool by the host's name), or must it still describe the mechanism without naming the host?

CONTRIBUTING.md's Development section describes settings.toml without its [slots] table or plugin_dir and would say nothing of file-backed values or the new rule. Is that section rewritten in this milestone alongside CLAUDE.md and docs/, or left out of scope?

docs/ways-of-using-cairn.md lists three --effort values for Antigravity while the installed agy --help lists five. Does this milestone correct that page's Antigravity command-line facts from the same hands-on check, or is that left out of scope?
